{{Other uses|Socle (disambiguation){{!}}Socle}}
In [[mathematics]], the term '''socle''' has several related meanings.

==Socle of a group==
In the context of [[group theory]], the '''socle of a [[group (mathematics)|group]]''' ''G'', denoted soc(''G''), is the [[subgroup]] generated by the [[minimal normal subgroup]]s of ''G''. It can happen that a group has no minimal non-trivial [[normal subgroup]] (that is, every non-trivial normal subgroup properly contains another such subgroup) and in that case the socle is defined to be the subgroup generated by the identity. The socle is a [[direct product of groups|direct product]] of minimal normal subgroups.{{sfn|Robinson|1996|loc=p.87}}

As an example, consider the [[cyclic group]] '''Z'''<sub>12</sub> with [[generating set of a group|generator]] ''u'', which has two minimal normal subgroups, one generated by ''u''<sup>4</sup> (which gives a normal subgroup with 3 elements) and the other by ''u''<sup>6</sup> (which gives a normal subgroup with 2 elements). Thus the socle of '''Z'''<sub>12</sub> is the group generated by ''u''<sup>4</sup> and ''u''<sup>6</sup>, which is just the group generated by ''u''<sup>2</sup>.

The socle is a [[characteristic subgroup]], and hence a normal subgroup. It is not necessarily [[Transitively normal subgroup|transitively normal]], however.

If a group ''G'' is a [[finite group|finite]] [[solvable group]], then the socle can be expressed as a product of [[elementary abelian]] [[p-group|''p''-group]]s. Thus, in this case, it is just a product of copies of '''Z'''/''p'''''Z''' for various ''p'', where the same ''p'' may occur multiple times in the product.

==Socle of a module==
In the context of [[module theory]] and [[ring theory]] the '''socle of a [[module (mathematics)|module]]''' <math>M</math> over a [[ring (mathematics)|ring]] <math>R</math> is defined to be the sum of the minimal nonzero [[submodule]]s of <math>M</math>. It can be considered as a [[duality (mathematics)|dual notion]] to that of the [[radical of a module]]. In set notation,

:<math>\mathrm{soc}(M) = \sum_{N \text{ is a simple submodule of }M} N. </math>
Equivalently,
:<math>\mathrm{soc}(M) = \bigcap_{E \text{ is an essential submodule of }M} E. </math>

The '''socle of a ring''' <math>R</math> can refer to one of two sets in the ring. Considering <math>R</math> as a right <math>R</math>-module, <math>\mathrm{soc}(R_R)</math> is defined, and considering <math>R</math> as a left <math>R</math>-module, <math>\mathrm{soc}(_RR)</math> is defined. Both of these socles are [[ring ideal]]s, and it is known they are not necessarily equal.

* If <math>M</math> is an [[Artinian module]], <math>\mathrm{soc}(M)</math> is itself an [[essential extension|essential submodule]] of <math>M</math>.
In fact, if <math>M</math> is a [[semi-Artinian ring|semiartinian module]], then <math>\mathrm{soc}(M)</math> is itself an [[essential extension|essential submodule]] of <math>M</math>. Additionally, if <math>M</math> is a non-zero module over a left [[semi-Artinian ring]], then <math>\mathrm{soc}(M)</math> is itself an [[essential extension|essential submodule]] of <math>M</math>. This is because any non-zero module over a left semi-Artinian ring is a semiartinian module.
* A module is [[semisimple module|semisimple]] [[if and only if]] <math>\mathrm{soc}(M)=M</math>. Rings for which <math>\mathrm{soc}(M)=M</math> for all module <math>M</math> are precisely [[semisimple ring]]s.
* <math>\mathrm{soc}(\mathrm{soc}(M))=\mathrm{soc}(M)</math>. 
* <math>M</math> is a [[finitely cogenerated module]] if and only if <math>\mathrm{soc}(M)</math> is [[finitely generated module|finitely generated]] and <math>\mathrm{soc}(M)</math> is an [[essential extension|essential submodule]] of <math>M</math>.
*Since the sum of semisimple modules is semisimple, the socle of a module could also be defined as the unique maximal semisimple submodule.
* From the definition of <math>\mathrm{rad}(R)</math>, it is easy to see that <math>\mathrm{rad}(R)</math> [[annihilator (ring theory)|annihilates]] <math>\mathrm{soc}(R)</math>. If <math>R</math> is a finite-dimensional unital [[Algebra over a field#Generalization: algebra over a ring|algebra]] and <math>M</math> a finitely generated <math>R</math>-module then the socle consists precisely of the elements annihilated by the [[Jacobson radical]] of <math>R</math>.<ref>[[J. L. Alperin]]; Rowen B. Bell, ''Groups and Representations'', 1995,  {{isbn|0-387-94526-1}}, p. 136</ref>

==Socle of a Lie algebra==
In the context of [[Lie algebra]]s, a '''socle of a [[symmetric Lie algebra]]''' is the [[eigenspace]] of its structural [[automorphism]] that corresponds to the [[eigenvalue]]&nbsp;−1. (A symmetric Lie algebra decomposes into the [[direct sum of modules|direct sum]] of its socle and [[cosocle]].)<ref>[[Mikhail Postnikov]], ''Geometry VI: Riemannian Geometry'', 2001,  {{isbn|3540411089}},[https://books.google.com/books?id=P60o2UKOaPcC&q=socle&pg=PA98 p. 98]</ref>
